result.question:
Continue and complete the VERIFIED citation base for the introduction of a concise Radiology: Artificial Intelligence paper. Thesis: hospitals with surgical navigation (tracker registered to a preoperative/intraoperative 3-D scan) localise the vertebral level instrumentally; hospitals without it count vertebrae by hand across successive C-arm shots; a navigation built entirely from OR C-arm shots would close the gap. The reader is a neurosurgeon who also knows AI, so every sentence must carry a verified number.

ALREADY VERIFIED / IN THE BIBLIOGRAPHY (do NOT re-research; only extend): mody2008 (1 in 3,110; 50% of surgeons), groff2013, furuya2026 (0.12% registry, thoracic 0.42%), longo2012, devine2010, hsiang2011 (level counting; navigation not available everywhere), mayer2008, strong2021, jc2024, kwaan2006 (62% preventable), stahel2010, nhse2025, mehtsun2013, matthews2007, keil2024, mongardi2021, tan2023, siminski2023, childers2018, goodkin2004, machin2018, bettis2026, manbachi2018 + otake2012 (LevelCheck requires a preoperative CT/MR), ammerman2006 (15% initial wrong exposure), upadhyaya2012 (fiducial cost-effectiveness, UCSF), Macki 2014 (fiducial $1,237.55 fluoro / $1,267.03 CT vs vertebroplasty marking $3,195), desilva2018, levelcheck2012/2016, unberath2018/2019 (DeepDRR), grupp2020 (DeepFluoro), synthex2023, fluorosam2025, kwak2025, sxstitch2024, spineclue2024, vertxnet2024.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING, each with DOI/PMID, the exact quoted sentence, and where the number sits (table/figure/page):
1. UPADHYAYA 2012 (J Neurosurg Spine 16:280-284): the exact cost figures and conclusion wording — cost per patient of preoperative percutaneous fiducial placement, the comparison arm (intraoperative fluoroscopic localisation time / cost), the number of patients, and whether wrong-level events changed. Quote the abstract's Results and Conclusions sentences verbatim.
2. NAVIGATION ACCESS DISPARITY: verified capital cost figures for (a) Medtronic O-arm + StealthStation, (b) Brainlab Airo/Cirq/Loop-X, (c) Globus ExcelsiusGPS, (d) 7D Surgical, from peer-reviewed cost-effectiveness or health-technology-assessment papers (e.g., Dea 2016 Spine J cost-effectiveness of navigation; Al-Khouja 2015; Sanborn 2012; Malham 2022; Fichtner 2019; NICE/HTA reports), and the share of hospitals or spine surgeons with navigation access from surveys (AO Spine Global Spine Care survey, NASS/CNS surveys, Härtl 2013 "Worldwide survey on the use of navigation in spine surgery" World Neurosurg — quote its percentages; Lee 2020/2023 updates; rural vs urban US, LMIC).
3. ANY published system that names or counts vertebral levels on real intraoperative fluoroscopy WITHOUT a 3-D scan (no preoperative CT/MRI, no tracker): search "vertebra level identification fluoroscopy deep learning", "C-arm level localization neural network", "intraoperative radiograph vertebra labeling registration-free", 2018–2026. For each: modality, whether a 3-D scan was needed, the reported accuracy and its metric, and whether it was tested on real fluoroscopy. If none exists, state that explicitly with the searches performed.
4. RSNA Radiology: Artificial Intelligence current author instructions (2025/2026): Original Research word limit, abstract structure and limit, key points, figure/table limits, CLAIM 2024 requirement, data/code sharing statement requirements, page/reference limits. Quote the instruction page.
5. The C-arm exposure counts / time / dose consumed by manual fluoroscopic level localisation in the OR (any prospective measurement: number of shots, minutes, mGy or DAP per localisation), to size the problem quantitatively.

Return a structured report per item with the citation, the quoted passage, the number, confidence, and what could not be verified.

confirmed.claim: Upadhyaya 2012 is a retrospective case-control series of 26 patients with preoperative CT-guided percutaneous 5-mm fiducial screws versus a historical cohort of 26 patients localised with intraoperative fluoroscopy alone, in open or minimally invasive thoracic spine surgery (abstract Methods; J Neurosurg Spine 2012;16(3):280-284; DOI 10.3171/2011.3.SPINE10445; PMID 22054638; MeSH: Case-Control Studies, Retrospective Studies).
confirmed.quote: The authors compared a group of 26 patients who underwent preoperative (often outpatient) fiducial screw placement prior to open or minimally invasive thoracic spine surgery to a historical group of 26 patients who had intraoperative localization with fluoroscopy alone.

confirmed.claim: Wrong-level surgery events did NOT differ: there were zero wrong-level surgeries in both the fiducial arm (0/26) and the fluoroscopy-alone historical arm (0/26), so the paper does not demonstrate that fiducials reduce wrong-level surgery; the only reported benefit is reduced localisation fluoroscopy time (abstract Results).
confirmed.quote: In the treatment group of 26 patients, no complications related to fiducial screw placement occurred, and there was no incidence of wrong-level surgery. In comparison, there were no wrong-level surgeries in the historical cohort of 26 patients who underwent mini-open or open thoracic spine surgery without placement of a fiducial screw. However, the authors found that the intraoperative localization fluoroscopy time was greatly reduced when a fiducial screw localization technique was employed.

confirmed.claim: The abstract contains NO cost figure, no dollar amount, no minutes/seconds of fluoroscopy time, and no dose value; the fluoroscopy-time reduction is stated only qualitatively ('greatly reduced'). Therefore the bibliography annotation 'upadhyaya2012 (fiducial cost-effectiveness, UCSF)' cannot be sourced to this abstract; per-patient fiducial cost figures ($1,237.55 fluoro / $1,267.03 CT vs $3,195 vertebroplasty marking) belong to Macki 2014. Any numeric fluoroscopy time in the body text is unverified: full text is subscription-only (thejns.org 403; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex report no open-access PDF; citationCount 57-62).
confirmed.quote: There is a reduction in the amount of intraoperative fluoroscopy time needed for localization in the fiducial screw group.

confirmed.claim: Upadhyaya 2012 is a historical-control comparison, not a prospective cost-effectiveness study: 26 thoracic-spine patients with a preoperative CT-guided percutaneous 5-mm fiducial screw were compared with 26 historical patients localized by intraoperative fluoroscopy alone (verbatim Methods sentence from the publisher page, identical on Europe PMC and PubMed for PMID 22054638).
confirmed.quote: To avoid wrong-level surgery in the thoracic spine, the authors preoperatively placed a percutaneous 5-mm fiducial screw at the level of intended surgery using CT guidance. Plain radiographs and CT images with reconstructed views can then be referenced in the operating room to verify the surgical level, and the fiducial screw is easily identified on intraoperative fluoroscopy. The authors compared a group of 26 patients who underwent preoperative (often outpatient) fiducial screw placement prior to open or minimally invasive thoracic spine surgery to a historical group of 26 patients who had intraoperative localization with fluoroscopy alone.

confirmed.claim: The Conclusions make three claims — safe/efficient/accurate, outpatient CT-guided placement, and reduced intraoperative fluoroscopy time — and contain no cost, cost-effectiveness, or dose statement; any 'Upadhyaya cost figure' in the introduction is unsupported by this primary and should be re-attributed (Macki 2014 carries the dollar figures). The publisher's reference list shows the Discussion cites cost papers (a carpal-tunnel OR-vs-clinic cost/profit analysis and 'Is intraoperative CT of posterior cervical spine instrumentation cost-effective...' Clin Orthop Relat Res 469:1035-1041, 2011), so any cost argument in the paper is qualitative and second-hand.
confirmed.quote: The aforementioned technique for intraoperative localization is safe, efficient, and accurate for identifying the target level in thoracic spine exposures. The fiducial marker screw can be placed using CT guidance on an outpatient basis. There is a reduction in the amount of intraoperative fluoroscopy time needed for localization in the fiducial screw group.

confirmed.claim: Under 2013 CPT coding, preoperative gold fiducial implantation for thoracic level localization costs $1,237.55 under fluoroscopic guidance and $1,267.03 under CT guidance (abstract; verified verbatim via PubMed PMID 24963696 and Europe PMC, both indexing DOI 10.1179/1743132814Y.0000000413; the publisher page itself returned HTTP 403). The abstract uses a mid-dot decimal ('$1237·55'); render as $1,237.55.
confirmed.quote: Following 2013 Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) coding, the cost of vertebroplasty under fluoroscopic guidance, $3195·43, or under computed tomography (CT) guidance, $3232·54, is more than double the cost of the gold fiducial implantation - $1237·55 and $1267·03, under similar imaging techniques, respectively.

confirmed.claim: The comparison arm is percutaneous vertebroplasty (PMMA cement) marking of a thoracic level, costed at $3,195.43 under fluoroscopy and $3,232.54 under CT — more than double the fiducial cost. Note the comparator is another preoperative marking procedure, NOT intraoperative fluoroscopic counting; the paper gives no cost or time for the count-by-hand alternative.
confirmed.quote: In comparison to percutaneous vertebroplasty marking of thoracic spinal levels with polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) cement, implantation of the gold fiducial is technically facile with a minimal learning curve. The fiducial markers are also associated with significantly less financial resources.

confirmed.claim: PMID 22054637 is NOT Upadhyaya 2012; it resolves to Adogwa O, Parker SL, Shau DN, Mendenhall SK, Devin CJ, Cheng JS, McGirt MJ, 'Cost per quality-adjusted life year gained of laminectomy and extension of instrumented fusion for adjacent-segment disease', J Neurosurg Spine 2012;16(2):141-146, DOI 10.3171/2011.9.SPINE11419 (epub 2011-11-04). Journal of Neurosurgery. Spine, Volume 16, Issue 2, pages 141-146, February 2012 ... DOI: 10.3171/2011.9.SPINE11419 ... PMID: 22054637

confirmed.claim: The correct record for the fiducial paper (located by a Europe PMC author/journal/year search, not from the task's page) is Upadhyaya CD, Wu JC, Chin CT, Balamurali G, Mummaneni PV, 'Avoidance of wrong-level thoracic spine surgery: intraoperative localization with preoperative percutaneous fiducial screw placement', J Neurosurg Spine 2012 Mar;16(3):280-284, PMID 22054638, DOI 10.3171/2011.3.SPINE10445; it compares 26 fiducial-screw patients against 26 historical fluoroscopy-only patients. Its verbatim Results/Conclusions sentences (cost per patient, localisation time) still need to be pulled from that record.
confirmed.quote: Title: Avoidance of wrong-level thoracic spine surgery: intraoperative localization with preoperative percutaneous fiducial screw placement. Authors: Upadhyaya CD, Wu JC, Chin CT, Balamurali G, Mummaneni PV. Journal: J Neurosurg Spine. 2012 Mar;16(3):280-284. DOI: 10.3171/2011.3.spine10445. PMID: 22054638. ... a group of 26 patients who underwent preoperative fiducial screw placement against a historical group of 26 patients

refuted.claim: Wrong-level events did NOT change: 0/26 wrong-level surgeries and 0 fiducial complications in the treatment arm and 0/26 wrong-level surgeries in the historical fluoroscopy-only arm; the only reported effect is that intraoperative localization fluoroscopy time was 'greatly reduced'. The abstract gives NO numeric fluoroscopy time and NO dollar cost; the '3 vs 15 minutes' figure used in the drafts (paper/qi_universal_protocol/main.tex:186, paper/focused/main.tex:176) sits in the paywalled full text (USD $45.00, 5 pages) and is currently only traceable through the Mongardi 2021 review, so it must stay co-cited with mongardi2021 or the full text must be obtained.

unverified.claim: Dea et al. 2016 costed a Medtronic O-arm + StealthStation S7 navigation system against conventional fluoroscopy from the hospital perspective, annuitising capital cost over 7 years at 3% and adding annual maintenance; the abstract characterises the technology as having 'substantial acquisition and maintenance costs' but does not state the absolute capital price in dollars (that figure is in the paywalled body).

The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of O-arm/StealthStation navigation was $15,961 per reoperation avoided, and at a reoperation cost of $12,618 the system only becomes cost saving for centres performing more than 254 instrumented spinal procedures per year — i.e., navigation is economically justified only at high-volume centres.

The authors' conclusion is that the high acquisition and maintenance costs of navigation are offset only by reoperation costs at high-volume centres with similar case complexity — the stated conditionality underpins the navigation-access-disparity argument.

The total annual cost of a Medtronic 3-D navigation platform for spine (O-arm hardware plus StealthStation8 software) was taken as $414,634, from a single-center pricing contract (Salinas Valley Memorial Healthcare System finance-committee minutes, June 2022; the paper's ref 17). The authors state the contract is representative of other public contracts but that pricing varies by facility and is not generally public.

Break-even annual spine case volume to justify the platform is 158 procedures if private payers reimburse 0% for revisions and 352 if they reimburse 100%; against 2019 CMS discharge data from 1,226 US inpatient spine centers, 61% (0% scenario) and 86% (100% scenario) of US inpatient facilities cannot make a business case for 3-D navigation. Note the paper's own Results summary sentence gives 163 rather than 158 (internal inconsistency; abstract, body and Discussion all say 158). The per-procedure gross-margin deltas driving this are $2,634 (0%) and $1,180 (100%).

In the worldwide AOSpine survey, only 11% of responding spine surgeons used computer-assisted navigation routinely, despite navigation systems being widely distributed in North America and Europe (verbatim from the PubMed abstract, Results; PMID 22469525, DOI 10.1016/j.wneu.2012.03.011).

The three main reasons non-users gave for not using navigation were lack of equipment, inadequate training, and high cost; routine users cited accuracy, facilitation of complex surgery, and reduced radiation exposure (abstract, Results).

Access to navigation was regionally unequal: 38% of the 677 respondents had access overall, 70% in North America, 42% in Europe, 42% in Asia Pacific, and 14% in Latin America, with no African respondents. NOTE: the Härtl full text is paywalled (ScienceDirect/ResearchGate 403); these regional figures were verified only from a secondary citing paper (Prevalence of spine surgery navigation techniques and availability in Africa, Ann Med Surg 2021, PMC8346523, ref. 29), not from Härtl's own tables. 677 is consistent with 3348 x 20% response rate.

In the 2023 AO Spine global survey (424 respondents, 9.9% response rate, 46% orthopaedic surgeons / 32% neurosurgeons), only 49% of surgeons reported occasional or frequent use of spinal navigation, and 34% had never used intraoperative 3-D navigation on a real patient. This is surgeon-reported use, not a hospital census, and the low response rate is a selection-bias caveat.

Free-hand fluoroscopy remains the majority technique for pedicle screw insertion worldwide: 57% (n = 243) use free-hand fluoroscopy and 35% (n = 148) use free-hand, versus 42% (n = 177) using navigation for screw insertion (Results section; respondents could select more than one technique).

Navigation access is sharply stratified by national income: 70% (n = 162) of high-income-country respondents versus 24% (n = 46) of low- and middle-income-country respondents use spinal navigation routinely or occasionally (p < 0.001). Robot ownership/use was 33% (n = 76) HIC vs 15% (n = 28) LMIC. Regional sample: Europe 37% (n = 155), Asia/Middle East 30% (n = 128), North America 15% (n = 65), South America 12% (n = 49), Africa 6% (n = 24).

In a 2021 convenience-sample e-survey of 113 African spine surgeons (neurosurgery and orthopaedics, 15 countries), fluoroscopy was available to 96.5% of respondents, whereas stereotactic navigation with intraoperative CT was available to only 8.8% and stereotactic navigation without intraoperative CT to 31.9%.

Cost of equipment was the dominant barrier to navigation access in Africa, cited by 94.7% of respondents, with lack of trained staff to service (63.7%) or run (60.2%) the equipment next; 98.2% reported at least one barrier.

The paper's Discussion restates the Härtl 2013 worldwide survey (677 spine surgeons) as finding 38% overall access to computer-assisted navigation, 70% in North America, 42% in Europe, 42% in Asia Pacific and 14% in Latin America; this is a secondary restatement and the primary Härtl paper (World Neurosurg 2013) should be quoted directly for the intro.
